Native check: English

Native speaker? Each line below is from the book. Read it and its question, then choose Correct if it is fine as it is, Needs change if it is not (and write how you would say it), or Not sure. Answer as many lines as you like.

Round 9 of 14. After you send, the next round has more lines.

You don't need to have read the book. The grey lines above each line show what comes just before it; only the line marked at the side is being checked.

  • Maman (mother), Baba (father) and -jan after a name (dear) are kept from Persian on purpose, like other Persian words such as beit and ghazal.
  • Some characters swear, speak crudely or mispronounce words on purpose; the question says so when it matters.
Line 1

The light of my dreams turned on

Now you are gone

The light of my dreams now blinks

In his poem the light flickers now that she is gone. Does 'now blinks' work for that?

Line 2

I hold no hope of your return

But if your path should bring you near

come into my dreams one more time

I don't think my dreams believe you're gone

This is the last line of Amir's love poem. Does it end the poem well, as poetry?

Line 3

Now you are gone

The light of my dreams now blinks

I hold no hope of your return

A line from Amir's love poem. Does it read naturally as poetry?

Line 4

The light of my dreams now blinks

I hold no hope of your return

But if your path should bring you near

A line from Amir's love poem. Does it read naturally as poetry, not stiff?

Line 5

…is carrying bread, toward Enghelab Square. I reach the entrance to the University of Tehran. I was late. The classroom was full and the latecomers were seated on the floor around the edges. Right by the door I found an empty spot and sat down. On the board, in fine handwriting, they had written:

One may write upon all things

This poem is written on a classroom board. Does its first line read as poetry?

Line 6

One may write upon all things

except on water

and if you cross the sea

write upon the water with your own blood

A poem on a classroom board. Does this line read naturally as poetry?

Line 7

will know that

lovers and

drunkards and

the burned ones

In the poem, 'the burned ones' means people consumed by love. Is that clear?

Line 8

will know that

lovers and

drunkards and

the burned ones

have passed this way.

This is the poem's last line. Does it close the poem well?

Line 9

You can read it two ways. If we take Hafez to be the summit of ambiguity, I'd say this single mesra is the – the su-summit of ambiguity in Hafez's ow-own words.

Nervous and excited, Amir stammers as he explains a line of poetry. Does the stammering read naturally?

Line 10

Eskandar, without changing his Buddha-like pose, said:

– What are you seeking to understand, Fly? The derivative? Meaning? Or the meaning of the derivative? Or the derivative of meaning?

Eskandar, a self-styled philosopher, lectures a struggling student. Does his mock-profound wordplay come through?

Line 11

Farid said:

– Awesome, Elder of the Tavern. That's perfect for Arasteh.

Farid gives Amir the nickname 'Elder of the Tavern' from a Hafez reading. Does it sound like a dorm nickname?

Line 12

Hooman was writing something in the book with a pen and said:

– Haha, Elder of the Tavern, Eldie, perfect. You hit the mark, Leopard Farid.

Hooman shortens the nickname 'Elder of the Tavern' to 'Eldie'. Does that sound like a natural nickname?

Line 13

Farid said:

– He's Taverny, truly and honestly.

Farid coins a second short form of the nickname. Does 'Taverny, truly and honestly' sound natural from him?

Line 14

Sajad said:

– Objectively, just because we arrived a few days late, these Tehran kids, who only got into AmirKabir thanks to localization, act like we're the ones who came in through a quota, not them. Objectively.

Sajad complains that Tehran students treat them as if they got in unfairly. Does this read naturally?

Line 15

Hooman said:

– Yeah. Don't let this Arasteh fool you; goofy as he is, his Konkoor rank was seventy-four.

Hooman brags about Amir's top rank in the national entrance exam. Does 'goofy as he is' sound natural?

Line 16

Sajad said:

– They killed Gaddafi. Objectively, come watch the video.

Sajad's habit word 'Objectively' pops up even here. Does it sound like a funny verbal tic?
